query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a compositionally complex, initially single-phase high-entropy alloy, high strain rate deformation induces dynamic, dislocation-assisted diffusion that drives selective elemental segregation (e.g., Cr, Ni, Mn) to grain boundaries. This segregation causes local compositional heterogeneities that reduce grain boundary cohesion, thereby triggering brittle behavior—a mechanism distinct from the conventional static grain-boundary precipitation observed in traditional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with uniformly distributed elements.
generation.intervention: Perform in situ tensile testing with controlled variation of applied strain rate (low versus high) under ambient and moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: Comparative experiments under service-relevant conditions: ambient and slightly elevated temperatures; low strain rates serve as the baseline, while high strain rates represent high energy-deformation scenarios.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions experiencing dynamic elemental segregation and potential nanoclustering forming nanoscale embrittling features that weaken the intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: At high strain rates, enhanced dislocation activity promotes accelerated diffusion and segregation of specific constituent elements along grain boundaries. The resulting local compositional changes weaken the grain boundary bonding and lower its resistance to cracking, leading to a transition from ductile to brittle failure modes.
generation.predicted_outcome: For high strain rate deformation, one should observe increased signatures of elemental segregation at grain boundaries (via APT) and microstructural evidence of embrittlement (via EBSD), coupled with reduced ductility and an increased propensity for intergranular brittle fractures compared to the low strain rate baseline.
generation.baseline: Under low strain rate deformation, the HEA maintains uniform grain boundary chemistry and exhibits high ductility with minimal evidence of segregation-induced embrittlement.
generation.boundary: These observations are expected within the strain rate and temperature range relevant to demanding engineering service; phenomena outside these ranges (e.g., at extreme temperatures or strain rates) may invoke additional mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold strain rate needed to trigger significant dynamic segregation and the quantitative extent of the segregation effect remain uncertain—further kinetic diffusion studies are needed to refine these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ tensile tests on the HEA sample at both low and high strain rates while simultaneously performing EBSD to track grain orientation changes and APT to detect grain boundary compositional variations. Assess the mechanical response (ductility and yield strength) and fracture surfaces for evidence of brittle failure.
measurements: Grain boundary elemental composition via APT
Fracture surface morphology (brittle vs. ductile characteristics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the strain rate does not lead to measurable grain boundary elemental segregation or if the mechanical behavior (ductility and fracture mode) remains similar to that at low strain rates, then the hypothesis—linking dynamic segregation to brittle behavior—is falsified.

In contrast to carbides and nitrides, intermetallic compound–induced embrittlement at room temperature can be relieved at high temperatures because plastic codeformation between these compounds and the matrix can reduce stress concentration and, thus, delay crack initiation (). Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution. occupying_moves.technique: in situ tensile testing with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and atom probe tomography (APT)
occupying_moves.conditions: Comparative tests on the initially single‐phase HEA at low versus high strain rates under ambient and moderately elevated temperatures to mimic service boundaries

chosen.technique: in situ tensile testing combined with EBSD and APT
chosen.conditions: Performing controlled tensile experiments on the compositionally complex, single‐phase HEA at varying strain rates (low vs. high) and temperatures (ambient and service‐relevant elevated temperatures) to capture the onset of deformation‐induced grain-boundary segregation and associated microstructural transitions
chosen.why: This approach directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that brittle behavior in HEAs emerges from strain‐induced compositional alterations (i.e., segregation at grain boundaries) not typically observed in conventional alloys. By systematically varying the strain rate—and thus the deformation energy input—it distinguishes between conventional intermetallic precipitation behaviors and a newly proposed mechanism for toughness degradation in HEAs, leveraging standard materials characterization and mechanical testing techniques in the field.
